Scant

/SKANT/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Scant means barely sufficient — so little that it falls short of what is needed.

Scant means barely sufficient — so little that it falls short of what is needed. The detective had only scant evidence: a single blurry footprint by the gate.

Worked Example

The teacher's proposal received scant attention at the crowded staff meeting; only two colleagues even looked up.

Scant fits because the amount of attention was far less than the proposal needed — barely any at all.

Antonyms

ample

plentiful

How Strong Is It? — slim → scant → nonexistent

slim vs. scant

slim vs. scant: A slim supply is small but might still stretch far enough; a scant supply falls short of what's actually needed.

nonexistent vs. scant

nonexistent vs. scant: Scant evidence is at least some evidence; nonexistent evidence is none at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — scant

Root — scant: from Old Norse skamt, the neuter form of skammr, 'short' — a shortness that became 'too little'

Put it together

Put it together: Scant comes from the Old Norse skamt ('short'), brought to England by Norse speakers. A word for physical shortness stretched into today's meaning: an amount cut short — barely enough.

Use the root in a new word: scanty

Use the root in a new word: scanty: The explorer's scanty notes left historians guessing about most of the journey.

Word Building

Word Choice

Slightly formal

Scant most often sits right before an abstract noun: scant attention, scant evidence, scant regard, scant hope. It's a close cousin of meager, another word in this unit — both mean 'barely enough,' but scant stresses falling just short of a needed amount, while meager stresses thin, inadequate quality (a meager meal). Scant can even mean 'just barely' with measurements: 'a scant teaspoon of salt.'
